item.title: secretsource — a secret from a reference
item.description:
Where does a PIN come from, when it must not sit in a file? A reference names where a secret lives; secretsource.Open fetches it. The reference holds no secret, so it may sit in a flag, a script or a shell history.

go get github.com/go-authn/secretsource@v0.12.0
s, err := secretsource.Open(ctx, "keepassxc:https://fido.invalid/yubikey-5c")
if err != nil { ... }
defer s.Close() // overwrites the bytes
use(s.Bytes())
Reference Reads
file:PATH a regular file readable by its owner alone (Unix: mode 0600 or stricter; Windows, since v0.7.0: an access list that grants no read or write right to anyone but the owner, SYSTEM and the Administrators group); one trailing newline is stripped; a file that is empty, or holds only a line ending, is refused with ErrEmpty (since v0.6.0), and a FIFO is refused as not a regular file
keychain:SERVICE/ACCOUNT a macOS Keychain generic-password item
secretservice:SERVICE/ACCOUNT a freedesktop Secret Service item with attributes service=SERVICE, account=ACCOUNT (GNOME Keyring, KWallet, KeePassXC’s Secret Service integration)
secretservice:KEY=VALUE[,KEY=VALUE...] the one Secret Service item carrying all those attributes; several matches are refused
keepassxc:URL the KeePassXC entry whose URL field is that URL (https://NAME.invalid/... is a good, never-resolving choice); two entries with the same URL are refused as ambiguous
systemd-creds:NAME (Linux, since v0.8.0) a systemd credential, returned byte for byte: no trailing-newline stripping, unlike file:. First the file NAME in $CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY (placed by LoadCredential=, LoadCredentialEncrypted=, SetCredentialEncrypted=); else NAME or NAME.cred in /etc, /run, /usr/lib credstore.encrypted, decrypted by systemd-creds decrypt. Refused with ErrUnavailable on other systems

file: does not follow a symbolic link (since v0.9.0). A link at the last component of the path, dangling or not, is refused: on Unix the file is opened with O_NOFOLLOW, on Windows with FILE_FLAG_OPEN_REPARSE_POINT and any reparse point is refused (a cloud-files placeholder too: point at a plain local copy). On Unix the file must also be owned by the calling user; root is not exempt. Migrating: point at the real file (readlink -f PATH). A symbolic link in a directory earlier in the path still works.

keepassxc:by-uuid/... and keepassxc:by-path/... are refused: KeePassXC 2.8.0 crashes when a lookup finds an entry with no URL.

No scheme runs a command: a flag must never be able to start a process. A reference with no scheme is refused, not guessed to be a path (file: is how a path is written). A secret longer than 4096 bytes, or an empty one from a manager or a file:, is refused (ErrEmpty), and a call ends with its context (2 minutes when it has no deadline) even while the manager waits for you to unlock it.

systemd credentials

Grammar, exactly: systemd-creds:NAME, the scheme in lower case, a colon, then the credential name as given to LoadCredential=, LoadCredentialEncrypted= orsystemd-creds encrypt --name=, for example systemd-creds:smtp. NAME is a plain file name of 1 to 255 bytes: no / (so no path), not . or .., no control character, and no .cred suffix (the suffix belongs to the file; smtp finds smtp or smtp.cred).

  • The file in $CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY is opened with O_NOFOLLOW, must be a regular file owned by root or the caller, with no access for “other” (group bits are accepted: systemd gives a User= service a root-owned 0440 file with an ACL); the directory likewise. A symlink or a loose mode is refused.
  • Otherwise systemd-creds decrypt --name=NAME PATH - is run directly: no shell,an empty environment, the secret read from standard output only, at most 4096 bytes, ended with the context. A non-root caller tries --user (systemd 256 or later) first.
  • No trimming: a trailing newline, NUL bytes and non-UTF-8 bytes are kept, so seal a password with printf %s.
  • Measured on systemd 257 (Debian 13) with --with-key=host; not measured with a TPM2 key. A failed decryption returns ErrUnavailable and says the credential may need re-sealing.
  • PCR binding: --tpm2-pcrs= defaults to none. A bare --tpm2-pcrs=7 can lock every credential after a firmware or shim update or a vTPM migration. Prefer--with-key=host+tpm2, a signed PCR policy (--tpm2-public-key, PCR 11), orsystemd-pcrlock, and keep a copy of the secret to re-seal from.

KeePassXC

KeePassXC is reached through its browser-integration protocol, on macOS and Linux; Windows is not implemented yet. Since v0.6.0, on Unix, the socket is refused when it is a symbolic link or when its directory is owned by another user or writable by group or others, and the uid of the connected peer is checked after the dial; the legacy $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/org.keepassxc.KeePassXC.BrowserServer symlink is no longer followed (the real socket under app/org.keepassxc.KeePassXC/ is).

Since v0.6.1, the association file (the fallback store, used when neither the macOS Keychain nor a Secret Service is there) is written to a new temporary file in the same directory and renamed onto the final name, so a symbolic link left at that name is replaced, not followed, and a file of looser mode comes out 0600. On Unix the directory is checked first, as the socket’s is: owned by this user, not writable by group or others, not a symbolic link; otherwise nothing is written.

Since v0.8.1, that write is done byharden/privfile v0.2.0. On Windows the file now gets an owner-only protected access list, as in go-authn/kinit v0.3.2, and the directory is checked again at the write, as well as before it.

  1. In KeePassXC, enable Settings > Browser Integration.
  2. Associate this machine once per database, and approve it in KeePassXC: 
    go install github.com/go-authn/secretsource/cmd/secretsource@latest
secretsource keepassxc associate
  3. Create the entry and fill its URL field withhttps://fido.invalid/yubikey-5c (any URL no other entry uses: the reference is that URL). Check the reference without printing the secret: 
    secretsource check 'keepassxc:https://fido.invalid/yubikey-5c'

The first read of an entry shows KeePassXC’s access dialog.

Used by fido --pin-from (see fido) and by theca --pin-from, --password-from and --recovery-from.

Taking a secret from a command-line flag: secretsource/secretflag

A secret passed as a flag value is visible in ps. The secretflag package gives a command the pair --<name> (deprecated, warns on stderr) and--<name>-from <ref>, mutually exclusive, with the reference resolved bysecretsource.Open:

var password string
b := secretflag.Add(cmd, "password", &password, "the admin password") // cobra
// or: secretflag.AddStd(fs, os.Stderr, "password", &password, "the admin password", "p")
// ... after parsing:
if err := secretflag.Resolve(ctx, b); err != nil { return err }

Add registers the pair on a cobra command, AddStd on a standard-libraryflag.FlagSet (with aliases such as -t); Resolve reads the references.Available since v0.10.0.

AddFrom registers only --<name>-from, with no deprecated plain twin, for a secret introduced after the plain flag was deprecated. AddFromList registers a repeatable --<name>-from; Resolve appends every resolved secret to a*[]string, in order (key rotation). Both trim, refuse an empty secret and keep the value out of errors, like Add. Available since v0.12.0.

Storing a secret: secretsource store

No entry has to be made by hand. secretsource store REF [--group G] [--login L] [--replace] [--generate N] writes the secret for keychain:,secretservice:SERVICE/ACCOUNT, secretservice:KEY=VALUE and keepassxc:URL:

secretsource store 'keepassxc:https://fido.invalid/yubikey-5c'
secretsource store 'keepassxc:https://fido.invalid/yubikey-5c' --generate 24
printf '%s' "$PIN" | secretsource store keychain:fido/yubikey-5c

The secret is typed twice with echo off, or read from standard input when that is not a terminal; it is never taken from an argument or the environment.--generate N draws N letters and digits and prints nothing secret. An existing entry is refused unless --replace (for KeePassXC that updates that entry, found by its URL). file: is refused.

For keepassxc: it uses the browser protocol’s set-login, so the entry always carries the URL that finds it again, and a duplicate is looked up by URL. The login defaults to the URL’s host (--login), the group is KeePassXC-Browser Passwords unless --group names one below the root, and --title is refused because KeePassXC 2.8.0 ignores it. KeePassXC shows its own dialogs.

Deleting a secret: Delete

Delete(ctx, ref) is the counterpart of Store, so a caller that keeps a token in the keychain can remove it on logout. Available since v0.11.0.

  • keychain: and secretservice:SERVICE/ACCOUNT remove the item. When a Secret Service lookup matches several items the result is ErrAmbiguous and nothing is deleted.
  • keepassxc:URL uses the browser protocol’s delete-entry: KeePassXC asks for confirmation and moves the entry to its Recycle Bin, so the password stays in the database until the bin is emptied.
  • An absent entry is an error that is both ErrNotFound and fs.ErrNotExist,so “already gone” can be treated as success on purpose.
  • file:, systemd-creds: and secretservice:KEY=VALUE are refused withErrNoDelete: this package never manages a file or credential it did not store, and an attribute lookup names no single item.

The entry is looked up before it is deleted. Nothing secret is returned or logged.

Reference

The README atgithub.com/go-authn/secretsource is the source of truth for this page.

item.title: sdcreds — systemd credentials, without systemd
item.description:
What if a service needs the credentials a systemd unit gets fromLoadCredentialEncrypted=, and there is no systemd? sdcreds reads and writes the systemd credential format(systemd-creds encrypt / decrypt) from Go, with a command line and a helper that gives an s6-supervised service the same $CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY.

Supported keys: null, host (/var/lib/systemd/credential.secret) andhost-scoped (--uid / --user). TPM2 and public-key credentials are recognised and refused with *UnsupportedModeError; nothing is guessed.

Install 

go install github.com/go-authn/sdcreds/cmd/sdcreds@latest

The version these pages describe is v0.3.0.

Command line 

sdcreds setup # create the host secret if missing
sdcreds encrypt --name=db-password plain.txt db-password.cred
sdcreds decrypt db-password.cred - # the name must match the file name

The same from Go:

host := sdcreds.HostKeyFile{} // $SYSTEMD_CREDENTIAL_SECRET or the default path
blob, err := sdcreds.Encrypt(secret, sdcreds.EncryptOptions{Key: sdcreds.IDHost, HostKey: host, Name: "db-password"})
text := sdcreds.Armor(blob, sdcreds.ArmorWidth) // what systemd-creds prints
raw, _ := sdcreds.Unarmor([]byte(text))
plain, md, err := sdcreds.Decrypt(raw, sdcreds.DecryptOptions{HostKey: host, Name: &name})

s6 

sdcreds s6-run --service=web --user=svc --source=/etc/creds -- /usr/bin/web

s6-run decrypts every file of --source before mounting anything, mounts a per-service tmpfs (nodev,noexec,nosuid,nosymfollow,noswap, mode 0700, size and inode count bounded; ramfs if the kernel lacks those options), writes the plaintext 0400 owned by the service user, remounts it read-only, setsCREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY, then starts the service in a child that drops privileges (no_new_privs, an empty capability set) and waits for it.

  • s6-run is still the process that s6 supervises: it forwards TERM, INT,HUP, QUIT, USR1, USR2, ALRM and CONT to the service, exits with its status (128 plus the signal number if a signal killed it), hands on the descriptors it was given, and the service is killed if s6-run dies.
  • The credentials are taken away when the service ends, and before s6-run fails if the program cannot be executed.
  • The mount lives in a private namespace by default (--unshare=false turns that off), so it disappears with the service.
  • A credential sealed with the null key is refused unless --allow-null is given, and one that carries no name is always refused.
  • sdcreds s6-finish --service=web unmounts lazily and removes the directory;it is idempotent. With --unshare=false, a SIGKILL of s6-run leaves the mount in place until s6-finish runs: put it in the finish script of the service.
  • At most 1024 credentials and 16 MiB per service. Linux only; elsewhere the commands report ErrUnsupported.

The key files named by --secret and --machine-id-file must be root-owned and not writable by group or others, and so must every directory above them up to/. The key file is opened once, without following a final link, and the key is wiped from the memory of s6-run when it is done with the credentials. Only the child takes the identity of the service; s6-run and all its threads stay root.

Keeping a capability: --keep-cap 

sdcreds s6-run --service=vpn --user=svc --source=/etc/creds --keep-cap=CAP_NET_ADMIN -- /usr/bin/vpn

The flag is repeatable and comma-separated (--keep-cap=CAP_NET_ADMIN,CAP_NET_RAW or one flag each) and has no default: without it the service runs with every capability set empty.

It is an allowlist of seven capabilities, none of them root-equivalent or able to read or write the credential tmpfs or to signal s6-run:CAP_NET_ADMIN, CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE, CAP_NET_RAW, CAP_NET_BROADCAST,CAP_IPC_LOCK, CAP_WAKE_ALARM and CAP_BLOCK_SUSPEND. Any other capability,or a name that is not a capability, is an error that names the allowlist,reported before the key is read or anything is mounted.

The service has, in its bounding, permitted, inheritable, effective and ambient sets, exactly the kept capabilities and nothing else. no_new_privs stays on,and the securebits are 0x3 (SECBIT_NOROOT set and locked). s6-run’s own privileges are unchanged.

CAP_NET_ADMIN acts on the network namespace the service runs in, which is the host’s unless the service is started in a network namespace of its own(--unshare only gives it a private mount namespace): there it can change interfaces, routes and the firewall. Run such a service in its own network namespace when that matters.

sdcreds run: OpenBSD and Linux 

sdcreds run --service=web --user=svc --source=/etc/creds [--class=daemon] -- /usr/local/bin/web

run decrypts the sealed files of --source, makes them visible to the program as read-only files owned by --user under $CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY, runs it as that user and removes them when it ends. On Linux it is s6-run with the same flags. --check runs every refusal and decrypts nothing (use it in an rc.drc_pre). A refusal exits with status 2 and happens before the host key is read. On OpenBSD the files live in a memory file system (MFS) mounted for the service and zeroed at the end:

  • There is no mount namespace. While the program runs, the credentials are visible to every process that can reach the directory, and root can always read them.
  • The host key is /etc/sdcreds/host.key, owned by root, mode 0600; any other mode or owner is refused. Create it withsdcreds setup --path /etc/sdcreds/host.key, then chmod 600 it. The machine id is sysctl hw.uuid. --secret and --machine-id-file override both and go through the same ownership and mode checks.
  • --user is never root: uid 0, gid 0 and any supplementary group 0 are refused, in run and in the library (s6.Run, delivery); there is no flag to allow it. The program must be an absolute, normalised path that the user can execute.
  • Killing sdcreds kills the program and unmounts, even with SIGKILL. A helper process holds the service lock and watches sdcreds; on any end it kills everything the service user runs (by real uid, so a program that calledsetsid does not escape) and then unmounts. The kill is decided by root: the helper stops every process it finds, reads the process table again until it no longer changes, then sends SIGKILL, and repeats until the user has no process. A process whose effective uid only is the service user’s is counted as busy, so the start is refused, but it is not killed. When a process survives the 20 s budget, the helper still unmounts (the secrets go), reports the failure and exits non-zero. A user is owned by one delivery at a time (the.uid-<N>.lock in /var/run/sdcreds), and run refuses a user that already has other processes: give the service its own user. If sdcreds and the helper both die, sdcreds sweep [--base DIR] [--service S] (or the next start of the service) removes the leftover. When the release fails after the program ends,sdcreds exits with status 70 (or the program’s own status when that was already a failure) and says why on stderr.
  • Swap must be encrypted. run refuses to start whensysctl vm.swapencrypt.enable is 0, cannot be read, or does not exist. There is no flag to override it. In the library, s6.Config needs a ReadSource (the command gives the trust-walked reader), or s6.Run refuses.
  • The embedded file-system images are pinned: the sha256 of eachdelivery/images/ffs-<N>MiB.gz is checked before the helper decompresses it.
  • --class is looked up in /etc/login.conf.d/<class> first, then/etc/login.conf; login.conf.db is not consulted. The resource limits of the class are applied to the program, only ever lowering what it would have, and a class that cannot be read or parsed is a refusal. Priority and umask are not applied; the program gets umask 077.
  • The program’s environment is an allow-list: PATH (a fixed default),CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY, LANG, TZ, TERM and LC_*. Descriptors above 2 are closed before it runs.
  • Memory. The plaintext is in the memory of the sdcreds process for a short time. mlockall cannot be used from a Go process on OpenBSD (measured on 8.0), so protection is vm.swapencrypt.enable (checked at start), core dumps off and kern.nosuidcoredump. A crash dump taken by an administrator can still contain the plaintext.
  • --keep-cap is Linux only.

docs/openbsd/authn_bridge in the repository is an rc.d script that runs go-authn/bridge this way. The delivery is also a library, package delivery.

Interoperability

Both directions are tested against the real systemd-creds 262.2, built from the v262.2 tag (no distribution package).

  • testdata/systemd-v262.2 holds 44 credentials written by systemd-creds (null,host and host-scoped; with and without a name; no, past and future not-after;0 B, 1 B and 64 KiB payloads; five tampered variants), and manifest.json records what systemd-creds itself answered for each of 272 decryption attempts(right and wrong name, before and after not-after, with and without --uid).The library gives the same answer, with the same class of error, for every one.
  • With a fixed IV, Encrypt reproduces systemd’s bytes exactly.
  • In the container, systemd-creds decrypt opens what Encrypt wrote, and the command line passes the same round trip in both directions.
docker build -t sdcreds-interop docker
docker run --rm --privileged -e SDCREDS_REQUIRE_SYSTEMD=1 -e SDCREDS_S6_INTEGRATION=1 \
 -v "$PWD":/src/sdcreds -w /src/sdcreds sdcreds-interop \
 sh -c 'echo 0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef > /etc/machine-id && go test -count=1 ./...'

Without SDCREDS_REQUIRE_SYSTEMD=1 the tests that need the binary are skipped;CI sets it, so an absent binary is a failure there. The 1 MiB boundary is covered by the library tests only, not by interop vectors.

Deviations from systemd

  • A host secret whose machine id does not match is refused (ErrHostKeyMachine); systemd removes it.
  • --with-key=auto means host: there is no TPM2 here.
  • A credential sealed with the null key has no secrecy: sdcreds decrypt refuses it on every machine unless --allow-null is given (systemd instead consults the TPM2 and SecureBoot state; that library policy,SystemNullPolicy, is not used by the CLI).
  • SDCREDS_MACHINE_ID_FILE (encrypt, decrypt, setup) points at another machine id file. s6-run ignores it and SYSTEMD_CREDENTIAL_SECRET: its key comes from the default files, or from --secret and --machine-id-file.
  • A variable IV size is accepted when reading, as in systemd; this library always writes 12 bytes.
  • The secret is opened without following a final symlink, and must be a regular file with one link and mode 0400, as systemd requires.

Safety

Every length is checked before it is used, before anything is allocated, and on both sides of its bound; credentials are limited to 1 MiB (as systemd) and the host secret to 16 MiB. The parsers are fuzzed in CI with the corpus committed,and govulncheck runs in CI. The README has no performance table yet: the measurement is deferred, an open item and not a result.

Reference

The README atgithub.com/go-authn/sdcreds is the source of truth for this page. See the module’s LICENSE.
